verdicts.quote: Method readBytes() reads a 32-bit unsigned integer as length (line 86), then allocates a byte array without size validation: `byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength];` (line 88). The condition `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE` (line 87) allows allocation up to 2,147,483,646 bytes.
verdicts.why: F02 is exactly the D1 mechanism: an attacker-controlled length field read off the wire (the 32-bit unsigned length) is used directly as the size of a newly allocated byte[], and the allocation happens up front with no check that the stream actually holds that many bytes. F02's stated exploit is that allocation itself (OutOfMemoryError from a gigabyte-sized buffer for a payload that need not exist), which is the attacker-controlled-size-buffer-allocated-before-payload-verified mechanism, not something merely mentioned in passing.

verdicts.quote: Method readFieldValue() (line 158) recursively calls itself indirectly: case 'F' (line 181) calls readTable() which calls readFieldValue() (line 150); case 'A' (line 184) calls readArray() which calls readFieldValue() (line 245). No recursion depth limit is enforced.
verdicts.why: F01 is exactly the D2 mechanism: the decoding routines readFieldValue/readTable/readArray call one another in a cycle, nothing tracks or bounds how deep the cycle goes, and the nesting depth of the attacker-supplied AMQP payload drives the depth until the stack is exhausted. That mutual recursion without a depth counter is what F01 says is exploitable, not an incidental mention.
